The Great Depression is an example of what happens when you treat labor as a free market good. The Combine Harvester made most farmers obsolete and there was a glut of labor competing for every other job. Under capitalism when the price of a good falls, people typically stop producing it. But with labor, people still need to earn money for food and housing. When the price of labor falls, they work harder to make the same amount of money, increasing the supply of labor further. It's a viscous feedback loop and the Great Depression wasn't the first time it has happened.

The usual solution to it was war (see Cottin Gin and the US Civil War) but that had already been tried in WW1. However, World War 1 was less lethal than wars of the past. so there was still a large surplus of laborers around in the 1930s. Thus we tried something different: Labor rationing. The 40 hour workweek and Unions split the smaller amount of work up among more people. Europe did not have this change to labor and thus they fell into World War 2. Japan and South Korea never got this change, and thus they've turned into a strange dystopia where people work themselves to death.

Capitalism does not play nicely with a labor surplus and technology has creeped up on labor to the point where we are nearing a tipping point once more.
